1. The user selects a .json file from disk; files that are not valid JSON show the message "Not a valid graph file" and change nothing.

3. Every node must have a string "id" and a "kind" that is one of the 28 ontology kinds; nodes with an unknown kind are kept but flagged in the health panel.
4. Edges whose source or target id does not exist are dropped and counted in a toast reading "N edges dropped".
5. After a successful import the graph is shown and autosaved to localStorage.
6. The whole import should feel snappy.

results.caseTitle: Precise criteria with one vague tail
results.input:
Acceptance criteria for the "Import graph" feature in Bropilot Studio:
1. The user selects a .json file from disk; files that are not valid JSON show the message "Not a valid graph file" and change nothing.
2. The file must contain a top-level "nodes" array and a top-level "edges" array; if either is missing, show "Missing nodes or edges" and change nothing.
3. Every node must have a string "id" and a "kind" that is one of the 28 ontology kinds; nodes with an unknown kind are kept but flagged in the health panel.
4. Edges whose source or target id does not exist are dropped and counted in a toast reading "N edges dropped".
5. After a successful import the graph is shown and autosaved to localStorage.
6. The whole import should feel snappy.

results.input:
Acceptance criteria for the "Import graph" feature in Bropilot Studio:
1. The user selects a .json file from disk; files that are not valid JSON show the message "Not a valid graph file" and change nothing.
2. The file must contain a top-level "nodes" array and a top-level "edges" array; if either is missing, show "Missing nodes or edges" and change nothing.
3. Every node must have a string "id" and a "kind" that is one of the 28 ontology kinds; nodes with an unknown kind are kept but flagged in the health panel.
4. Edges whose source or target id does not exist are dropped and counted in a toast reading "N edges dropped".
5. After a successful import the graph is shown and autosaved to localStorage.
6. The whole import should feel snappy.

results.caseTitle: Assumption vs test plan, hidden threshold
results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

results.caseTitle: Assumption vs test plan, hidden threshold
results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

results.caseTitle: Assumption vs test plan, hidden threshold
results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

Three-way match rule: PO qty = Goods Receipt qty = Invoice qty (within 2% tolerance).

results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

This article argues that logical pluralism, the view that more than one logic is correct, cannot account for the normativity of logic for rational belief. We consider whether a pluralist can say which consequence relation an agent ought to follow when two logics disagree. We conclude that pluralism collapses either into monism or into relativism about validity.

results.caseTitle: Air pollution and childhood asthma cohort
results.input: We followed 14,000 children from birth in a prospective birth cohort to estimate the association between early-life exposure to fine particulate matter and incident asthma by age seven. Exposure was modelled from residential addresses, and hazard ratios were adjusted for parental asthma, smoking and neighbourhood deprivation. Each 5 microgram per cubic metre increase was associated with a 14% higher hazard of asthma.

results.caseTitle: Finite model property of a modal logic
results.input: We establish that the modal logic K4.3 with a universal modality has the finite model property and is decidable in exponential time. The argument uses a filtration technique adapted to the universal modality together with a tableau calculus for which we prove soundness and completeness. We also show that the complexity upper bound is tight by reduction from a tiling problem.

This paper examines how astronomers at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, debated and standardised the recording of transit observations in the nineteenth century. Based on observatory logbooks, correspondence and committee minutes, it shows how disputes over the "personal equation" shaped norms of objectivity. It argues that standardisation was driven as much by institutional rivalry as by instrument improvement.

Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

results.caseTitle: Assumption vs test plan, hidden threshold
results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

RULE (Invoicing Policy §T.2, modelled on EU VAT invoicing rules): "Every VAT invoice issued to a business customer must show the supplier's VAT identification number."

results.caseTitle: Assumption vs test plan, hidden threshold
results.input:
Assumption A3 (Protopilot, Assumptions pass). Prediction: freelance designers who receive a clickable prototype will complete the "send invoice" task without help in under 90 seconds. What would change my mind: if fewer than 3 of 5 participants finish unaided, or if the median time exceeds 90 seconds. Alternative explanation: designers already know the invoicing tool, so success reflects familiarity, not the prototype. Decision informed: whether to build the invoice flow before the reminders flow.

Test plan T3 (Prototype & test pass). Task: "Send an invoice to a client for 400 dollars." Intended participants: freelance designers who have never used the invoicing tool, to control for the familiarity alternative. Prototype: the clickable invoice flow v2. Scenario: participant is alone on a laptop with a screen recorder; the facilitator may not speak after the instructions are read. Observation rule: record whether the participant reaches the confirmation screen unaided and the time from first click to confirmation. Sample: 5 participants. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 participants finish unaided with a median time under 90 seconds.

results.caseTitle: Air pollution and childhood asthma cohort
results.input: We followed 14,000 children from birth in a prospective birth cohort to estimate the association between early-life exposure to fine particulate matter and incident asthma by age seven. Exposure was modelled from residential addresses, and hazard ratios were adjusted for parental asthma, smoking and neighbourhood deprivation. Each 5 microgram per cubic metre increase was associated with a 14% higher hazard of asthma.

This study asks how neighbourhood segregation and the structure of personal social networks shape trust in vaccination among recent immigrant communities. Using a survey of 900 households and network data on who people consult for health advice, we find that dense, co-ethnic networks transmit both trust and scepticism. We discuss how institutional distrust is socially reproduced across generations.

This paper examines how astronomers at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, debated and standardised the recording of transit observations in the nineteenth century. Based on observatory logbooks, correspondence and committee minutes, it shows how disputes over the "personal equation" shaped norms of objectivity. It argues that standardisation was driven as much by institutional rivalry as by instrument improvement.

results.input:
RULE (Internal Control SOD-3, SOX-style): "An employee who creates or modifies a vendor master record in the ERP system may not approve invoices or payments to that vendor."

PRACTICE: While the accounts payable manager was on leave, an AP clerk created a new vendor record for a cleaning contractor and, to avoid a late-payment fee, approved the vendor's first invoice of €2,300 herself. The manager reviewed and signed off the transaction retrospectively when she returned a week later.

results.caseTitle: Screening blood draw before signed consent
results.input:
RULE (Trial Protocol §6.1, modelled on ICH-GCP): "Written informed consent must be obtained from each participant before any study-specific procedure is performed, including screening tests done only to determine eligibility."

PRACTICE: A potential participant arrived for a screening visit. The research nurse explained the study verbally and the participant agreed orally, so the nurse drew a blood sample for the study's eligibility panel at 09:10. The participant read and signed the written consent form at 09:45 the same morning.

results.caseTitle: Upfront recognition of an annual support contract
results.input:
RULE (Revenue Policy §5, summarising IFRS 15 / ASC 606 step 5): "Revenue is recognised when, or as, the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer. A performance obligation satisfied over time, such as a stand-ready service provided evenly across a contract term, is recognised over that term."

PRACTICE: On 1 January a software vendor signed a 12-month technical support contract for €120,000, under which it stands ready to answer the customer's support tickets throughout the year. The customer paid the full amount on 1 January, which is non-refundable. The vendor recognised the full €120,000 as revenue in January.

results.caseTitle: Invoice compliant with quoted VAT-number rule; other rule breached
results.input:
RULE (Invoicing Policy §T.2, modelled on EU VAT invoicing rules): "Every VAT invoice issued to a business customer must show the supplier's VAT identification number."

PRACTICE: A supplier issued a VAT invoice to a business customer. The invoice shows the supplier's name, address and VAT identification number, the invoice date, a sequential invoice number, the goods supplied and the VAT charged. It was issued 45 days after the goods were delivered, whereas national VAT law requires invoices to be issued within 15 days of the supply.

RULE (Digital Accessibility Policy §A.3, modelled on WCAG 2.x SC 1.4.3): "Body text on customer-facing web pages must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background."

PRACTICE: The redesigned checkout page uses grey body text (#747474) on an off-white background (#FAFAFA). The measured contrast ratio is 4.48:1. The design lead signed it off, noting that the ratio rounds to 4.5:1, that no user can perceive the difference, and that the text passed an informal readability check with five colleagues.

RULE (Data Retention Policy §9.2): "CVs and application data of unsuccessful candidates must be deleted within 6 months after the recruitment process closes, unless the candidate has given explicit written consent to be kept in the talent pool, in which case the data may be retained for up to 24 months from the date of that consent."

PRACTICE: A candidate was rejected for a data analyst role when that recruitment closed on 1 February 2024. At rejection she ticked an unticked box on a signed web form reading "I consent to Acme keeping my CV in its talent pool for future roles". On 1 April 2025, 14 months later, her CV is still held in the talent pool.

results.caseTitle: Marketing emails based on a pre-ticked box
results.input:
RULE (Privacy Policy §3.1, modelled on GDPR Art. 4(11) and Recital 32): "Customer personal data may be used for direct-marketing emails only where the customer has given prior opt-in consent. Consent must be given by a clear affirmative act; silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity do not constitute consent."

PRACTICE: The online checkout page shows a box, ticked by default, labelled "Send me offers and news by email". Customers can untick it before paying. The company sends its weekly promotional newsletter to every customer who completed checkout with the box still ticked, and every newsletter contains a one-click unsubscribe link.

results.caseTitle: Screening blood draw before signed consent
results.input:
RULE (Trial Protocol §6.1, modelled on ICH-GCP): "Written informed consent must be obtained from each participant before any study-specific procedure is performed, including screening tests done only to determine eligibility."

PRACTICE: A potential participant arrived for a screening visit. The research nurse explained the study verbally and the participant agreed orally, so the nurse drew a blood sample for the study's eligibility panel at 09:10. The participant read and signed the written consent form at 09:45 the same morning.

results.caseTitle: Invoice compliant with quoted VAT-number rule; other rule breached
results.input:
RULE (Invoicing Policy §T.2, modelled on EU VAT invoicing rules): "Every VAT invoice issued to a business customer must show the supplier's VAT identification number."

PRACTICE: A supplier issued a VAT invoice to a business customer. The invoice shows the supplier's name, address and VAT identification number, the invoice date, a sequential invoice number, the goods supplied and the VAT charged. It was issued 45 days after the goods were delivered, whereas national VAT law requires invoices to be issued within 15 days of the supply.

RULE (Digital Accessibility Policy §A.3, modelled on WCAG 2.x SC 1.4.3): "Body text on customer-facing web pages must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background."

PRACTICE: The redesigned checkout page uses grey body text (#747474) on an off-white background (#FAFAFA). The measured contrast ratio is 4.48:1. The design lead signed it off, noting that the ratio rounds to 4.5:1, that no user can perceive the difference, and that the text passed an informal readability check with five colleagues.

RULE (Employee Handbook §3.4, modelled on the US FLSA): "Non-exempt employees must be paid at one and one-half times their regular rate of pay for all hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek."

PRACTICE: A non-exempt warehouse associate worked 39 hours in the workweek of 10–16 June. Payroll paid every hour that week at the associate's regular hourly rate.

results.caseTitle: Marketing emails based on a pre-ticked box
results.input:
RULE (Privacy Policy §3.1, modelled on GDPR Art. 4(11) and Recital 32): "Customer personal data may be used for direct-marketing emails only where the customer has given prior opt-in consent. Consent must be given by a clear affirmative act; silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity do not constitute consent."

PRACTICE: The online checkout page shows a box, ticked by default, labelled "Send me offers and news by email". Customers can untick it before paying. The company sends its weekly promotional newsletter to every customer who completed checkout with the box still ticked, and every newsletter contains a one-click unsubscribe link.

results.caseTitle: Upfront recognition of an annual support contract
results.input:
RULE (Revenue Policy §5, summarising IFRS 15 / ASC 606 step 5): "Revenue is recognised when, or as, the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer. A performance obligation satisfied over time, such as a stand-ready service provided evenly across a contract term, is recognised over that term."

PRACTICE: On 1 January a software vendor signed a 12-month technical support contract for €120,000, under which it stands ready to answer the customer's support tickets throughout the year. The customer paid the full amount on 1 January, which is non-refundable. The vendor recognised the full €120,000 as revenue in January.

results.input:

Conclusion: "A person who tests positive almost certainly (above 90% probability) has the disease."
